name: Reticulocyte
short_description: Young, anucleate red blood cell freshly released from bone marrow; still carries residual ribosomal RNA that stains as a reticular network. Matures into a full erythrocyte within 1-2 days.
reference_text: A reticulocyte is an immature erythrocyte that has just left the bone marrow for peripheral blood. It has already extruded its nucleus (during the orthochromatic normoblast stage), so it is anucleate like the mature red cell it will become, but it still retains residual ribosomal RNA and free ribosomes, plus scattered remnants of mitochondria, Golgi membranes and endoplasmic reticulum left over from its nucleated precursor. When stained supravitally (new methylene blue or brilliant cresyl blue) this residual RNA precipitates into a characteristic filamentous-granular meshwork -- the 'reticulum' that gives the cell its name -- visible under light microscopy as a fine blue net or scattered blue-black granules inside an otherwise haemoglobin-pink cell. On a routine Wright-Giemsa smear the same RNA gives the cell a faint blue-grey tinge over the pink of haemoglobin, called polychromasia. Reticulocytes are slightly larger than mature erythrocytes and are often not yet a perfect biconcave disc -- membrane remodelling (spectrin-actin cytoskeleton reorganisation, loss of surface area) that produces the final biconcave shape happens during this maturation window. The cytoplasm is still dominated by haemoglobin, which is the main determinant of the cell's overall pink-red colour and its main job (oxygen transport) is already active. Maturation takes about 1-2 days, partly in the marrow sinusoids/spleen and partly in circulation: residual ribosomes, mitochondria and other organelle remnants are cleared by autophagy and by exosome release (and, in part, by 'pitting' in the spleen), and globin synthesis from residual mRNA gradually stops as ribosomes are lost. Clinically, the reticulocyte count/percentage (normally roughly 0.5-2.5%, with ~1% being a commonly cited healthy average of circulating red cells) is a key marker of erythropoietic activity -- how fast the bone marrow is manufacturing new red cells -- rising in blood loss, haemolysis or after erythropoietin treatment, and falling in marrow failure or nutritional deficiency anaemias.
sources: Junqueira's Basic Histology, ch. 12 (Blood) -- reticulocyte morphology and supravital staining

labels.en: Residual RNA (reticulum, revealed by supravital stain)

do_not_draw: No nucleus -- the reticulocyte has already ejected it at the normoblast stage; do not draw it as a nucleated precursor.

No dense, abundant organelles like a secretory cell (rich rough ER/Golgi) -- only sparse, degenerating remnants of mitochondria/Golgi/ER, because the cell is being cleared of organelles, not building them up.
No true perforation/hole through the disc -- the biconcave shape is a thinned centre, not a torus with an actual opening.
No granules like a platelet or neutrophil (no alpha-granules, no specific/azurophilic granules).
Not perfectly flat/uniform like a mature erythrocyte -- it is slightly larger, plumper and less perfectly biconcave (still remodelling its shape).

The residual-RNA reticulum is only visible with supravital staining (new methylene blue/brilliant cresyl blue) -- render it as a fine internal filamentous/granular network only in the SEM/textbook/3d/watercolor interior views, not as an external feature.
